parts: Lesson 3: Sole Proprietorship, Partnership and Hindu Undivided Family — Summary

A business owned, financed, managed and controlled by one person, who takes all the profit and bears all the risk. Examples: a grocery shop, a beauty parlour, a small travel agency. Characteristics: ease of formation (few legal formalities, no registration needed); single ownership (one man's capital); one-man control; unlimited liability — if business assets fall short, the owner's personal property is used to pay creditors; undivided risk; secrecy; no separate legal entity (owner and business are the same); lack of continuity — death or illness can end it.

Advantages: easy to form and close; quick decisions; direct motivation (all profit is the owner's); flexibility; secrecy; personal contact with customers and employees; generates self-employment. Limitations: limited capital (one man's savings and borrowings); limited managerial ability; unlimited liability discourages expansion; uncertain life; not suitable for large-scale business.

Unlimited liability worked out: if business assets are ₹5 lakh, liabilities ₹10 lakh and personal property ₹6 lakh, creditors get the full ₹10 lakh — ₹5 lakh from the business and ₹5 lakh from personal property.

The relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all (Indian Partnership Act, 1932). Members are partners and together a firm. Characteristics: at least two persons (maximum 50 under the Companies Rules; the NIOS text gives 20, 10 for banking); agreement — oral or written (the written one is the partnership deed); lawful business; sharing of profits and losses as agreed (equally if there is no deed); unlimited and joint liability; mutual agency — every partner is both an agent and a principal; utmost good faith; restriction on transfer of interest without consent of all; no separate legal entity; registration is optional; uncertain life — death, insolvency or retirement of a partner can dissolve it. Two people merely sharing the rent of a jointly owned godown are co-owners, not partners, because they carry on no business.

Contents of a partnership deed: name and address of the firm and partners; nature of business; capital contributed by each; profit-sharing ratio; interest on capital and drawings; salaries or commission to partners; rules for admission, retirement and death; method of settling disputes. Advantages: easy formation; more capital and combined skills; balanced decisions; sharing of risk; flexibility; protection of minority interests. Limitations: unlimited liability; uncertain life; limited capital; possible conflict among partners; non-transferability of interest.

Set up under the Limited Liability Partnership Act, 2008. An LLP is a body corporate with a separate legal identity from its partners and perpetual succession; the liability of partners is limited to their agreed contribution; it needs at least two partners (no maximum) and at least two designated partners, one of them resident in India; the rights and duties of partners are governed by the LLP agreement. It combines the flexibility of a partnership with the limited liability of a company.
Joint Hindu Family (Hindu Undivided Family) business

A business owned by the members of a Joint Hindu Family, governed by Hindu law and the law of succession — found only in India. Members are coparceners (traditionally male members; three successive generations; daughters are coparceners since 2005); membership is by birth (a minor can be a member), not by agreement. Features: management by the Karta (the eldest member), who has unlimited liability, while other coparceners' liability is limited to their share in the HUF property; no maximum number of members; continuity — it is unaffected by the death of a coparcener or even the Karta (the next senior male becomes Karta); registration not needed. Merits: assured economic security, quick decisions by the Karta, continuity, family pride and loyalty, limited liability of members. Limitations: limited capital and managerial skill, unlimited liability of Karta, scope for conflict, dominance of the Karta.
